subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy received morphine 4 mg IV 30 minutes ago for severe pain. The surgeon explained the procedure yesterday, but the form was never signed. The client is oriented and says, "Just give me the paper and I'll sign it." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Witness the client's signature, because the client is oriented and the surgeon has already explained
Hold the form and tell the surgeon that consent cannot be obtained right now
Ask the client's spouse, who holds health care power of attorney, to sign instead
Have the client repeat the risks back, then witness the signature

rationale.correct: Informed consent needs a client who is competent and not under the influence of sedating drugs. The nurse does not witness a signature that may be invalid; the surgeon is told.

perOption.a: Being oriented does not cancel the effect of an opioid given 30 minutes ago; consent signed now could be invalid.
perOption.b: Consent given under the influence of a sedating drug may not be valid; the surgeon decides how and when to obtain it.
perOption.c: The agent decides only when the client lacks capacity; a temporary drug effect is managed by waiting, not by substitution.
perOption.d: Checking understanding is the surgeon's role, and the opioid effect still makes the consent questionable.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize when a client can't give valid informed consent.

questions.stem: A client signed the consent form for a sigmoid colon resection yesterday. While the nurse is completing the preoperative checklist, the client asks, "Will I have to wear a bag on my stomach afterward? Nobody mentioned that." Transport is due in 30 minutes. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that a temporary colostomy is sometimes needed and is usually reversed later
Tell the client the surgeon will answer the question in the preoperative holding area
Notify the surgeon before premedication so the client's question is answered
Give the client the hospital's ostomy booklet to read before transport

rationale.correct: If a client shows they do not understand the procedure, the nurse stops the process and notifies the provider, who is responsible for informing the client.

perOption.a: Explaining the procedure and its possible outcomes is the surgeon's role, and the nurse cannot know this client's plan.
perOption.b: The client must be informed before sedation; waiting until holding risks proceeding without understanding.
perOption.c: The client is not fully informed; the surgeon must clarify before the procedure, and consent can be revisited.
perOption.d: Written material does not replace the surgeon's explanation of this client's procedure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a client doesn't fully understand a procedure after signing consent.

questions.stem: The nurse is precepting a new graduate on a surgical unit. Which statements about informed consent are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The provider who performs the procedure explains its risks, benefits and alternatives
The nurse's witness signature confirms that the client signed it and did so voluntarily
A client can withdraw consent at any time before the procedure, even after signing
An emancipated minor, such as a married 17-year-old, can give consent
Consent is signed before the client receives preoperative sedation
The nurse's witness signature confirms that the client understood the risks
A competent but anxious client's spouse can sign to spare the client the stress
A signed form allows the surgeon to add other procedures decided on during surgery

rationale.correct: Valid consent needs a competent client, full disclosure by the provider, understanding and voluntary agreement. The nurse witnesses the signature and may not take on the provider's duty to explain.

perOption.a: The person doing the procedure is responsible for disclosure.
perOption.b: The nurse witnesses the signature and voluntariness, not the client's understanding.
perOption.c: Consent can be withdrawn verbally or in writing until the procedure starts.
perOption.d: Emancipated minors are treated as adults for consent.
perOption.e: Sedating drugs can make consent invalid, so the form is completed first.
perOption.f: Confirming understanding is the provider's responsibility.
perOption.g: A competent adult gives their own consent; a family member cannot sign for convenience.
perOption.h: Consent covers the procedures disclosed, except for a true emergency.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the elements of informed consent and the nurse's role.

questions.stem: An unconscious adult with a ruptured spleen arrives in the emergency department after a car crash. Blood pressure is 74/40. No family can be reached, and the client carries no advance directive. How does the team obtain consent for emergency surgery?

options.text: Surgery waits until the police locate a relative who can give consent
The hospital asks a judge for an emergency court order before surgery
The nurse and the surgeon sign the consent form on the client's behalf
Surgery goes ahead under the emergency exception, and this is documented

rationale.correct: The emergency exception (implied consent) allows treatment needed to save life or limb when the client cannot consent and no one can consent for them.

perOption.a: Delaying lifesaving surgery would cause serious harm.
perOption.b: A court order is not needed and would delay emergency care.
perOption.c: Staff do not sign consent for a client.
perOption.d: When a life-threatening emergency prevents consent and no representative is available, consent is implied.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply implied consent in a life-threatening emergency.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a client who speaks Vietnamese and very little English. The client's 12-year-old daughter speaks English well and offers to help. A housekeeper on the unit also speaks Vietnamese. How should the nurse obtain the health history?

options.text: Ask the daughter to interpret, since the client trusts her
Ask the housekeeper to interpret during the admission interview
Use the hospital's telephone or video medical interpreter service
Use a translation app on the nurse's phone for the key questions

rationale.correct: Clients with limited English have a right to a qualified medical interpreter, in person, by phone or by video. Family members, children and untrained staff are not used.

perOption.a: Children may filter or not understand medical content, and the history may include sensitive topics.
perOption.b: Bilingual staff who are not trained interpreters may translate medical terms wrongly and breach privacy.
perOption.c: Qualified medical interpreters translate accurately and keep information confidential.
perOption.d: Apps are not reliable for health histories and are not a secure way to handle client information.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use a qualified interpreter for clients with limited English proficiency.

questions.stem: Ms. Grant, a client with metastatic breast cancer, has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order and is being treated for pneumonia. The client has said she wants all treatment except CPR and intubation. Which statement by a new nurse requires correction?

options.text: "We will keep giving her antibiotics and oxygen as prescribed."
"We can still call the rapid response team if her breathing gets worse."
"If her heart stops, we will not start chest compressions."
"Because she is DNR, she cannot go to the ICU for noninvasive ventilation."

rationale.correct: DNR means no CPR if the heart or breathing stops. All other care the client chooses, including intensive care, continues.

perOption.a: A DNR order does not stop other treatments the client wants.
perOption.b: Rapid response care short of CPR and intubation is consistent with her wishes.
perOption.c: This is exactly what the DNR order means.
perOption.d: DNR applies only to resuscitation; she can receive ICU-level care, including BiPAP, if she wants it.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Clarify what a DNR order does and does not cover.

questions.stem: A client on hemodialysis who is alert and oriented has named a daughter as health care power of attorney. After a long discussion with the nephrologist, the client says, "I want to stop dialysis." The daughter tells the nurse, "I'm the power of attorney, and I say dialysis continues." Whose decision should the nurse follow?

options.text: The daughter's, because she is the client's named health care agent
The client's, because the client has decision-making capacity
The nephrologist's, because stopping dialysis will end in death
The ethics committee's, because the client and agent disagree

rationale.correct: A durable power of attorney for health care takes effect only when the client cannot decide. A competent client may refuse life-sustaining treatment.

perOption.a: The agent decides only when the client cannot make decisions.
perOption.b: A competent client makes their own decisions; the power of attorney is not active while the client has capacity.
perOption.c: Providers advise, but they do not override a competent client's informed choice.
perOption.d: An ethics consult can help the family, but the competent client's decision stands.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respect a competent client's decisions over a health care agent's.

questions.stem: A client's valid living will states that the client declines mechanical ventilation. The client is now in respiratory failure and can't communicate. The client's son, who lives out of state, demands that the client be intubated. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Prepare for intubation while the provider talks to the son, then sort it out later
Tell the son firmly that the living will must be followed, then leave the room
Speak up for the documented wishes, and involve the provider and ethics team
Ask the son to bring the client's other children so the family can vote

rationale.correct: The nurse advocates for the client's known wishes in a valid advance directive and involves the provider and ethics team when the family disagrees.

perOption.a: Intubating against a valid directive violates the client's wishes and is hard to undo.
perOption.b: The client's wishes stand, but this ignores the son's distress and the team's role.
perOption.c: The nurse advocates for the client's stated wishes and brings in the provider and ethics resources to support the family.
perOption.d: Family members cannot override a valid advance directive by agreement or majority.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for a client's advance directive in a family conflict.

questions.stem: The nurse manager is reviewing privacy practices on a medical unit. Which action by a nurse violates client confidentiality?

options.text: Giving bedside handoff on a client in a private room, with the client's agreement
Mentioning a client's room number and new HIV result to a friend in the cafeteria line
Faxing a client's discharge summary to the client's primary care office
Reporting a new case of active tuberculosis to the local health department

rationale.correct: HIPAA allows sharing for treatment, payment, operations and legal requirements. Identifiable information is never discussed where others can overhear.

perOption.a: Bedside report with the client's participation is acceptable.
perOption.b: Discussing identifiable information where others can overhear breaches privacy, and HIV status needs special protection.
perOption.c: Sharing information for treatment is permitted.
perOption.d: Reporting certain communicable diseases is required by law.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize breaches of confidentiality.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is reviewing an electronic health record access report for the unit. Which access requires the charge nurse to follow up with the nurse involved?

options.text: A nurse opened the record of a client on another unit whom the nurse cared for last week
A nurse reviewed the record of an assigned client before taking report at the start of the shift
A nurse looked at a discharged client's record as part of an assigned fall-prevention audit
A nurse opened a client's record to check an allergy before the client was transferred in

rationale.correct: Access a record only when your current role in that client's care, or an assigned job duty, requires it. Concern or curiosity about a former client is not enough.

perOption.a: The nurse no longer has a care-related reason to see the record; curiosity about a former client is still a privacy violation.
perOption.b: This is a legitimate, care-related use.
perOption.c: Quality improvement work assigned by the facility is a permitted use.
perOption.d: Preparing to receive a client is a care-related reason.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify inappropriate access to health records.

questions.stem: A caller says she is a client's daughter and asks how her mother is doing after surgery this morning. The nurse does not recognize the voice. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give a brief update without any details, because the caller is family
Ask for the client's privacy code and check the authorized list first
Say politely that no one by that name is a client on this unit today
Transfer the call to the surgeon, who can decide what to share

rationale.correct: Before sharing information by phone, confirm that the client has authorized the caller, for example with a privacy code or a signed release.

perOption.a: The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is or whether the client allows disclosure.
perOption.b: Information is shared only with people the client has authorized, after their identity is checked.
perOption.c: Lying is not appropriate; the nurse can say they cannot share information.
perOption.d: The surgeon is bound by the same rules; the caller's authorization still has to be checked.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect client information during telephone inquiries.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the client bill of rights with a newly admitted client. Which rights should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Refusing treatment, including medications
Seeing and getting a copy of their own medical record
Privacy during care and examinations
Being told about their diagnosis, treatment and prognosis
Getting any medication they ask for
Choosing which staff document in their record

rationale.correct: Client rights include information, privacy, access to records, taking part in decisions and refusing treatment.

perOption.a: Competent clients may refuse any treatment.
perOption.b: Clients have the right to access their records.
perOption.c: Privacy and dignity are client rights.
perOption.d: Clients have a right to information about their care.
perOption.e: Clients take part in decisions, but providers prescribe based on clinical judgment.
perOption.f: Documentation is a legal requirement for everyone who gives care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify client rights in health care.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension and heart failure refuses the scheduled dose of metoprolol, saying, "That pill makes me dizzy when I get up." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Explain that metoprolol protects the heart and that skipping doses is dangerous
Ask more about the dizziness and check the client's pulse and blood pressure
Record the refusal and report it to the provider at the end of the shift
Offer the dose again in 30 minutes, after the client has rested in bed

rationale.correct: When a client refuses a medication, respect the refusal, explore and assess the reason, then document and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Teaching may help later, but it does not address the reason the client gave.
perOption.b: The client's reason may be an adverse effect such as bradycardia or orthostatic hypotension, which the provider needs to know about.
perOption.c: Documentation is needed, but a possible adverse effect should be assessed and reported promptly.
perOption.d: Repeated offers do not explore or address the reason for the refusal.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond appropriately to a client's medication refusal.

questions.stem: A client admitted with chest pain is alert and oriented. Troponin results are pending. The client says, "I'm going home to look after my dog, and you can't stop me." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Call security to keep the client on the unit until the troponin result is back
Explain the risks, notify the provider and offer the against-advice form
Take the client's clothes to the locker room so the client is less likely to leave
Tell the client that insurance will not pay for the stay if the client leaves

rationale.correct: A competent client may leave against medical advice. The nurse informs, notifies the provider, documents and does not restrain.

perOption.a: Holding a competent adult against their will can be false imprisonment.
perOption.b: The nurse informs the client of the risks, involves the provider and documents the event; the client may refuse to sign.
perOption.c: Hiding clothing is a form of restraint and false imprisonment.
perOption.d: This is coercive and often untrue.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a client leaving against medical advice.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing ethical principles with new nurses using examples from the unit. For each nursing action, choose the ethical principle it best shows.

rows.text: Respecting a Jehovah's Witness client's refusal of a blood transfusion
Turning an immobile client every 2 hours to prevent pressure injuries
Giving the last ICU bed by clinical need rather than insurance status
Telling a client honestly that a test result is not yet back

rationale.correct: Autonomy = self-determination; beneficence = doing good; nonmaleficence = avoiding harm; justice = fairness; veracity = truthfulness; fidelity = keeping promises.

perOption.r1:c1: Respecting a competent client's choice honors autonomy.
perOption.r1:c2: Beneficence is doing good; here the nurse honors a choice the nurse may not agree with.
perOption.r1:c3: Justice concerns fair distribution, not individual choices.
perOption.r2:c1: This is not about the client's choices.
perOption.r2:c2: Acting to benefit the client is beneficence.
perOption.r2:c3: This is not about fair allocation.
perOption.r3:c1: This is not about the client's own choice.
perOption.r3:c2: The focus is fairness between clients, not doing good for one.
perOption.r3:c3: Distributing scarce resources fairly is justice.
perOption.r4:c1: Honesty supports autonomy, but the principle shown is truthfulness.
perOption.r4:c2: Honesty may help the client, but the principle is truthfulness.
perOption.r4:c3: This is not about fair allocation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match nursing actions to ethical principles.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is seen in the emergency department for a forearm fracture. The nurse finds bruises of different colors on the back and buttocks. The parent says the child "falls a lot" and gives a different account of the fracture than the other parent did at triage. What is the nurse's responsibility?

options.text: Report suspected abuse to child protective services as the law requires
Ask the provider to order a skeletal survey and decide whether to report afterward
Interview the child alone first to confirm abuse before making any report
Document the findings and let the social worker decide whether a report is needed

rationale.correct: Injuries that don't match the history, bruises of different ages in protected areas and changing accounts must be reported. Nurses report on reasonable suspicion and are protected when reporting in good faith.

perOption.a: Nurses are mandated reporters; reasonable suspicion is enough to report, and the report is made promptly.
perOption.b: A skeletal survey may be ordered, but the duty to report does not wait for proof.
perOption.c: The nurse does not need to confirm abuse, and repeated interviews can harm the child and the investigation.
perOption.d: The social worker can help, but the mandated reporter's own duty to report remains.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Fulfill mandatory reporting duties for suspected child abuse.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with mild dementia comes to the clinic with bruises on both upper arms. The adult child who is the caregiver answers every question for the client and says the client bruises easily. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the caregiver to describe exactly how and when the bruises happened
Find a reason to interview the client alone, away from the caregiver
Call adult protective services before the client leaves the clinic
Document the bruises as a side effect of the client's daily aspirin

rationale.correct: When abuse is suspected, assess the client away from the possible abuser, then report as required.

perOption.a: The caregiver may be the abuser, and the client may not feel safe to speak.
perOption.b: A private interview gives the client a safe chance to disclose abuse.
perOption.c: Reporting is required if abuse is suspected, but first the nurse gathers more data safely.
perOption.d: This assumes the cause without assessment.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess safely for suspected elder abuse.

questions.stem: The nurse notices that a coworker smells of alcohol, has slurred speech and is preparing a client's 0900 medications. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Take the medication cup from the coworker and give the medications instead
Report the coworker to the charge nurse right away, before more care is given
Ask the coworker privately whether they have been drinking before the shift
Report the coworker to the state board of nursing after the shift ends

rationale.correct: Report suspected impairment at once to the supervisor so the nurse can be removed from client care; later steps follow facility policy.

perOption.a: This protects one client but leaves the impaired nurse caring for others.
perOption.b: Impaired practice puts clients at risk now and must be reported through the chain of command immediately.
perOption.c: Questioning the coworker delays action, and the coworker is likely to deny it.
perOption.d: The board may be involved later; the immediate step is to remove the risk to clients now.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a colleague who seems impaired at work.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes digoxin 2.5 mg orally once a day for a 76-year-old client with heart failure. The client's apical pulse is 74/min. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it and check the apical pulse first
Give 0.25 mg, because the order is almost certainly a decimal-point error
Hold the medication and contact the provider to clarify the dose
Ask the pharmacist to change the order to the usual dose of 0.125 mg

rationale.correct: The nurse is legally responsible for giving only safe doses; a questionable order is held and clarified with the prescriber, using the chain of command if needed.

perOption.a: This dose is about ten times the usual maintenance dose and could be fatal.
perOption.b: The nurse cannot change an order without the prescriber's clarification.
perOption.c: A dose outside the safe range is clarified with the prescriber before anything is given.
perOption.d: The pharmacist can help, but only the prescriber can correct the order.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Clarify an unsafe medication order.

questions.stem: A client's blood pressure is 82/48, and the nurse calls the provider, who gives a telephone order for a 500 mL normal saline bolus. Which action by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Write the order down and read it back in full for the provider to confirm
Repeat the drug name and volume aloud, then start the bolus straight away
Ask a second nurse to listen on the line instead of reading the order back
Start the bolus, then ask the provider to enter the order when on the unit

rationale.correct: Telephone and verbal orders are written down, read back in full and confirmed, then signed by the provider within the time set by policy.

perOption.a: Read-back of the complete order confirms accuracy and is required for telephone orders.
perOption.b: A partial repeat can miss the rate or route; the whole order is written and read back.
perOption.c: A second listener does not replace read-back confirmation.
perOption.d: The order must be written and confirmed when given, not left for later.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Receive telephone orders safely.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client who lives alone is admitted with a hip fracture and will have surgery tomorrow. When should the nurse start discharge planning?

options.text: On the day the client goes home
After surgery, once the client is walking
On admission
When the discharge order is written

rationale.correct: Discharge planning starts on admission.

perOption.a: Planning on the last day leaves no time to arrange services.
perOption.b: Planning can and should begin before surgery.
perOption.c: Discharge planning begins at admission so needs and services can be arranged in time.
perOption.d: Waiting can delay discharge or leave needs unmet.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify when discharge planning begins.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client who lives alone in a two-story house is being discharged 3 days after hip surgery. The client takes six medications at home and was started on enoxaparin in the hospital. Which actions should the nurse include in discharge planning? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange a home safety evaluation
Reconcile the home and hospital medication lists with the client
Arrange physical therapy after discharge
Confirm a follow-up appointment with the surgeon
Tell the client to stop every medication taken before admission
Postpone the plan until a family member can visit

rationale.correct: Safe discharge covers home safety, medication reconciliation, therapy, follow-up and support services.

perOption.a: A home assessment finds fall hazards and equipment needs.
perOption.b: Reconciliation prevents omissions, duplications and interactions, including with the new anticoagulant.
perOption.c: Continued therapy supports mobility and recovery.
perOption.d: Follow-up supports continuity and early detection of complications.
perOption.e: Home medications are reconciled, not stopped automatically.
perOption.f: The plan is made with the client, who is the decision-maker.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan a safe discharge for an older adult.

questions.stem: A client with a large sacral pressure injury will go home with a negative-pressure wound therapy device and needs dressing changes three times a week. The client's partner works full time. Which referral should the nurse request?

options.text: Home health nursing through the case manager
An occupational therapy evaluation at home
A hospice program for comfort care at home
Outpatient physical therapy visits twice a week

rationale.correct: Case managers coordinate services needed after discharge, such as skilled home nursing for wound care.

perOption.a: The case manager arranges skilled home nursing to manage the device and dressings.
perOption.b: OT does not manage wound care.
perOption.c: Hospice is for clients with a terminal illness who want comfort care.
perOption.d: PT does not manage wound dressings.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Coordinate home health services for ongoing skilled care.

questions.stem: A client on a ventilator after a severe traumatic brain injury has fixed, dilated pupils and no cough or gag reflex. The neurologist plans formal brain death testing this afternoon. The family is at the bedside. What should the nurse do according to policy?

options.text: Ask the family gently whether the client would have wanted to donate organs
Notify the organ procurement organization of the client's condition
Wait for the declaration, then raise donation
Discuss donation with the family together with the neurologist after testing

rationale.correct: Federal rules require prompt referral of imminent deaths to the organ procurement organization, whose trained staff approach the family.

perOption.a: Donation is raised with the family by trained requesters from the organ procurement organization.
perOption.b: Hospitals must refer imminent deaths to the OPO in a timely way so donation can be evaluated.
perOption.c: Waiting can make donation impossible, and the nurse is not the one who makes the request.
perOption.d: Families are approached by OPO staff, usually separately from the death declaration.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Follow the referral process for potential organ donation.

questions.stem: Just before giving a medication, the nurse notices the pharmacy dispensed the wrong drug, so the nurse doesn't give it. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Nothing more, because no harm reached the client
Report the near miss in the event reporting system
Document the near miss in the client's medical record
Tell the pharmacist privately and leave it there

rationale.correct: A just culture encourages reporting errors and near misses so system causes can be fixed.

perOption.a: Near misses show weaknesses in the system and should be reported.
perOption.b: Reporting near misses supports quality improvement and helps prevent future errors.
perOption.c: Event reports are not part of the medical record.
perOption.d: Informal communication skips the quality-improvement process.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Report near misses for quality improvement.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a new graduate's documentation for a client 2 days after a knee replacement. Highlight the entries that are inappropriate in the medical record.

segments.text: "0900: Client walked 30 m (100 ft) with a walker and standby assistance."
"1000: Client is lazy and refused to walk."
"1200: Client states, 'My pain is a 4 now.'"
"1300: Dr. Kim made an error with the dose again."

rationale.correct: Medical record entries are objective and factual, include the client's own words, and leave out incident reports and blame.

perOption.s3: Judgmental labels are not facts; chart the refusal and the client's words.
perOption.s5: The incident report is not mentioned in the record.
perOption.s9: Blame and opinions about others do not belong in the chart.
